drills.q: Implement strStr(): find the first occurrence of pattern P in text T in O(n+m), deterministically.
drills.a: KMP: build the failure function (lps array) on P in O(m), then scan T once in O(n), falling back to lps[j-1] on mismatch instead of restarting the pattern pointer.

drills.q: Why does resetting the KMP pattern pointer to 0 on every mismatch (instead of using lps) silently break the algorithm's complexity guarantee?
drills.a: It degrades KMP into the naive O(nm) algorithm -- it still produces correct matches, but loses the whole point: never re-reading text characters. The bug doesn't crash, it just erases the asymptotic benefit.

drills.q: Given a string, determine if it can be constructed by repeating a substring (Repeated Substring Pattern, LC 459), using KMP.
drills.a: Compute lps on the string itself; if n % (n - lps[n-1]) == 0, the string has period (n - lps[n-1]) and is fully periodic.

drills.q: You're building a content-deduplication service using Rabin-Karp rolling hash over user-uploaded text, with a small fixed modulus. What's the security risk and the fix?
drills.a: An attacker can construct many strings that collide under that specific known modulus, forcing O(m) verification on every window and degrading the service to O(nm) -- a denial-of-service vector. Fix: use a large randomly-seeded modulus at process start, or double hashing with independent random parameters.

drills.q: Find the longest common substring between two strings using hashing instead of the classic O(nm) DP. What's the technique and complexity?
drills.a: Binary search on candidate length L; for each L, compute rolling hashes of all length-L substrings of both strings and check for a common hash (with verification). O(n log n) total, using monotonicity: if a common substring of length L exists, one of length L-1 also exists.

drills.q: Given k patterns and one text, find all occurrences of any pattern efficiently. Why doesn't running KMP k times scale, and what's the right tool?
drills.a: Running KMP k times costs O(k*n + sum(pattern lengths)), worse than a single combined scan when k and n are large. The right tool is Aho-Corasick: a trie of all patterns with failure links (generalizing KMP's failure function to many patterns), giving a single O(n + sum(pattern lengths) + matches) scan.
